summary: Fine-tuning makes sense only after prompt engineering and RAG have provably hit a wall: the 2026 canonical sequence is prompt first (shape behavior at inference time), then RAG (inject fresh or proprietary knowledge), then fine-tune (bake patterns, style, or task skills into the weights). Choose fine-tuning when behavior remains inconsistent at scale, when you need a specific tone/format/domain skill baked in by default, or when latency and cost require a smaller specialized model rather than a large general one. RAG is better for knowledge that changes frequently, while prompting is the cheapest first stop for communication and formatting issues.
when_to_fine_tune: Behavior stays inconsistent at scale even after well-engineered prompts and a working RAG pipeline — you need patterns baked into the model's weights.
You need a consistent style, tone, format, or domain-specific skill as the model's default output rather than something coaxed per-prompt.
You want to shrink inference cost and latency by distilling a large model's behavior into a smaller, specialized fine-tuned model.
Your knowledge is relatively static (not rapidly changing facts, which RAG handles better) and you have a high-quality labeled dataset to train on.

tools.name: OpenAI Fine-Tuning API
tools.pricing_paid: Pay-per-token for training plus per-token inference on fine-tuned models; varies by base model (e.g. GPT-4o-mini and GPT-4.1 tiers).
tools.best_for: Instruction tuning and behavior/style adaptation on frontier closed models without managing infrastructure.

tools.name: Hugging Face AutoTrain
tools.pricing_paid: Pay for compute (GPU hardware from T4 to A100/H100) on Hugging Face infrastructure; autoscaling Inference Endpoints billed hourly.
features: Choice of GPU hardware and autoscaling policies
tools.best_for: No-code domain adaptation and experimentation across the broadest open-model catalog.

tools.name: Unsloth
tools.pricing_paid: Open-source (free); Pro/Enterprise tiers for multi-GPU and managed support.
features: Runs on a single consumer GPU / Colab
tools.best_for: Cost-efficient LoRA/QLoRA fine-tuning on limited or consumer GPU hardware.

tools.name: Axolotl
tools.pricing_paid: Open-source (free); you pay only for your own compute.
tools.best_for: Reproducible, configurable fine-tuning and RLHF-style tuning for practitioners who want full control.

tools.name: Amazon Bedrock Fine-tuning
tools.pricing_paid: Pay for training tokens plus provisioned throughput for hosting the custom model; billed via AWS.
features: Custom model import and continued pretraining
tools.best_for: Enterprise domain adaptation requiring AWS-native security, governance, and data residency.

tools.name: Vertex AI
tools.pricing_paid: Pay for tuning compute (node-hours) plus prediction/serving costs; billed via Google Cloud.
features: Model Garden with open + proprietary models
tools.best_for: Enterprise instruction tuning of Gemini and open models inside the Google Cloud ecosystem.

tools.name: Together AI
tools.pricing_paid: Fine-tuning priced per 1M tokens: $0.48 (LoRA up to 16B) to $8.00 (full fine-tune 70-100B); specialized models $5-$40 per 1M tokens plus minimum job charge; storage $0.16/GiB/month.
tools.best_for: Fine-tuning open models with fast, production-grade managed inference and transparent token pricing.

tools.name: LLaMA-Factory
tools.pricing_paid: Open-source (free); you pay only for your own compute.
features: Popular in open-source and research community
tools.best_for: Unified, low-friction fine-tuning and RLHF across many open models via UI or CLI.

tools.name: Modal
tools.pricing_paid: Serverless pay-per-second GPU compute (A10G/A100/H100 tiers); free starter credits.
tools.best_for: Developers who want flexible, code-first fine-tuning on on-demand serverless GPUs.

tools.name: Replicate
tools.pricing_paid: Pay-per-second for training and inference by GPU type; hosted fine-tunes billed on usage.
tools.best_for: Quick fine-tuning and instant deployment of open models via a simple API.
